faq.a: Some causes (e.g., untreated infections, hypothyroidism, severe malnutrition) are reversible with timely treatment; most structural or genetic causes improve with early therapy but are not fully reversible.
MRI provides better detail of cortical and white‑matter abnormalities without radiation, which is important for planning therapy.
faq.q: Why is MRI preferred over CT in these children?

faq.a: Refer for a comprehensive developmental assessment and begin targeted investigations based on history.
faq.q: What is the first step if a child fails the screening test?

exam: What bedside observations would suggest cerebral palsy versus simple motor delay? — Look for tone abnormalities (spasticity, dystonia), asymmetry, and persistent reflexes; simple delay shows normal tone.
A 3‑year‑old with HIV presents with regression of speech. Which investigations are essential? — HIV viral load, head MRI, and thyroid function; MRI to rule out HIV‑related encephalopathy.

How would you differentiate autism from hearing loss in a low‑resource setting? — Perform a simple otoacoustic emission test; if hearing is intact, assess social reciprocity and repetitive behaviours.
A child with suspected ADHD is hypertensive. Which medication should you avoid and why? — Avoid stimulants (methylphenidate) because they can raise blood pressure and increase cardiovascular risk.
Explain why a normal head ultrasound does not exclude a cortical malformation. — Ultrasound only visualises ventricles and large cysts; cortical dysplasia requires MRI.
What are the key components of early intervention for cerebral palsy in a district hospital? — Physiotherapy, positioning aids, caregiver training, and referral for orthopaedic assessment if needed.

A toddler with severe malnutrition shows developmental delay. What reversible factor should you address first? — Correct micronutrient deficiencies (iron, zinc, vitamin A) and provide therapeutic feeding.
Why is the GMFCS used instead of IQ for cerebral palsy severity? — GMFCS grades functional mobility, which directly guides therapy and prognosis, whereas IQ does not reflect motor ability.
ai.title: Developmental Disorders in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Developmental disorders encompass delays, intellectual disability, cerebral palsy, autism spectrum disorder and ADHD. They arise from genetic, prenatal, perinatal and post‑natal factors and require systematic assessment, targeted investigations and multidisciplinary management, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Use the Denver Developmental Screening Test or Ages and Stages Questionnaire for initial screening.
Confirm with formal assessment (e.g., Bayley Scales, WISC) for intellectual disability.
sections.p: A developmental disorder is a persistent deficit in achieving age‑appropriate milestones in cognition, communication, motor skills or social interaction, confirmed by standardized tools.

b: Intellectual disability: mild (IQ 50‑69), moderate (35‑49), severe (20‑34), profound (<20).
Cerebral palsy: GMFCS levels I‑V (I = walks without limitation, V = severe mobility limitation).
sections.p: Severity is graded by functional impact and IQ for intellectual disability, and by Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) for cerebral palsy.

b: Genetic syndromes (Down, Fragile X).
Maternal infections: malaria, HIV, syphilis, TORCH.
Perinatal hypoxia, birth asphyxia, prematurity.
Post‑natal: severe malaria, bacterial meningitis, untreated HIV, chronic malnutrition.
sections.p: Causes are grouped into genetic, prenatal (infection, toxin), perinatal (asphyxia, prematurity) and post‑natal (trauma, infection, malnutrition). In East Africa, infections and perinatal complications dominate.

b: Delay: failure to sit, crawl, speak by expected ages.
Intellectual disability: limited problem‑solving, adaptive skills.
Cerebral palsy: spasticity, dystonia, abnormal tone.
Autism: limited social reciprocity, restricted interests.
ADHD: inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity.
sections.p: Children may miss motor, language or social milestones, show poor eye contact, repetitive behaviours, or have attention‑deficit symptoms.
Investigations aim to identify aetiology, rule out treatable causes and guide management.

t.b: Detect structural brain lesions; MRI preferred if available, otherwise ultrasound for ventriculomegaly.
Identify metabolic disorders; treatable causes like hypoglycaemia or electrolyte imbalance.
Screen for perinatal HIV, a common cause of neurodevelopmental delay.
Detect congenital hypothyroidism, a reversible cause of delay.
Identify chromosomal abnormalities; if unavailable, rely on clinical dysmorphology.

b: Progressive loss of milestones.
Seizures or abnormal eye movements.
Severe malnutrition or failure to thrive.
Signs of raised intracranial pressure.
sections.p: Certain signs suggest urgent intervention or poor prognosis.

b: Treat infections (e.g., antiretroviral therapy for HIV, antibiotics for meningitis).
Start physiotherapy and occupational therapy early; use community‑based rehab when specialist services lack.
For autism, apply structured behavioural programmes (e.g., ABA) using locally trained workers.
ADHD: start low‑dose stimulant (e.g., methylphenidate) if available; avoid in uncontrolled cardiac disease.
Provide nutritional rehabilitation and vitamin supplementation (e.g., vitamin A, iron).
sections.p: Management combines cause‑specific treatment, early intervention, and supportive therapies.

b: Re‑assess milestones every 3‑6 months.
Ensure immunisation against measles, meningitis, and hepatitis B.
Promote exclusive breastfeeding, maternal nutrition, and safe delivery practices.
sections.p: Regular developmental surveillance and vaccination are key.

b: Hearing loss – check audiometry; treat with hearing aids.
Visual impairment – perform basic eye exam; correct refractive errors.
Childhood epilepsy – EEG to differentiate seizure‑related regression.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic developmental delay must be considered.

b: Normal head ultrasound does not exclude cortical malformations; MRI is needed if suspicion remains.
Thyroid tests can be transiently normal in early congenital hypothyroidism; repeat if clinical suspicion persists.
sections.p: Some investigations may be falsely normal.

whenToSeekHelp: New onset seizures, loss of previously acquired skills, signs of raised intracranial pressure, severe malnutrition, or any acute deterioration.
